animals.name: Domestic Dog
animals.dangerNotes: Generally friendly but can bite if threatened or provoked. Stray dogs may be aggressive.
animals.description: The domestic dog is a descendant of the grey wolf and is the world's most widely kept domestic animal. Bred over thousands of years into hundreds of distinct breeds, dogs serve as companions, working animals, and livestock guardians. Highly social and intelligent, they communicate through vocalisation, body language, and scent.
animals.funFact: Dogs have an extraordinary sense of smell estimated to be 10,000-100,000 times more acute than that of humans.
aiNotesOrWarnings: LifeSpanWildYears is a feral/stray-population estimate, not a verified source figure.

animals.name: Domestic Cat
animals.dangerNotes: Scratches and bites can cause infection. Feral cats may act defensively.
animals.description: The domestic cat is a small, agile carnivore and one of the most popular pets worldwide. Descended from the North African wildcat, cats were first domesticated around 10,000 years ago in the Near East. They are skilled hunters with retractable claws, excellent night vision, and a highly flexible body.
animals.funFact: Cats spend approximately 70% of their lives sleeping - around 13-16 hours per day.
aiNotesOrWarnings: LifeSpanWildYears reflects feral colony averages (predation, disease, traffic), not owned pets.

animals.name: Domestic Rabbit
animals.dangerNotes: Can scratch or bite when handled roughly. No significant threat to humans.
animals.description: The domestic rabbit is descended from the European wild rabbit and has been selectively bred into over 300 recognised breeds. Rabbits are popular as both pets and livestock, valued for their meat, fur, and companionable nature. They are social animals that communicate through ear position, body posture, and thumping.
animals.funFact: Rabbits cannot vomit - their digestive system is a one-way street, making a high-fibre diet essential.
aiNotesOrWarnings: primaryFoods reflects a generalist grazer/browser diet; captive rabbits should have hay as the dietary staple rather than pellets alone.

animals.name: Domestic Cow
animals.dangerNotes: Cows with calves can be protective and charge. Bulls are unpredictable and dangerous.
animals.description: Domestic cattle are large ruminant mammals descended from the now-extinct aurochs, domesticated approximately 10,000 years ago. They are among the most economically important livestock in the world, raised for beef, milk, leather, and as draught animals. Cattle are highly social, living in herds with clear social hierarchies.
animals.funFact: Cows have a near-360-degree field of vision and can detect odours from up to 10 kilometres away.
aiNotesOrWarnings: LifeSpanWildYears based on feral/free-ranging herds (e.g. Chillingham-type); domestic herd lifespan is usually shorter due to culling, not longevity.
primaryFoods generalised across beef and dairy husbandry; exact feed mix varies significantly by operation type.

animals.name: Domestic Pig
animals.dangerNotes: Sows with piglets can be aggressive. Large boars may charge and bite.
animals.description: The domestic pig is descended from the Eurasian wild boar and is one of the most numerous large mammals on Earth. Pigs are highly intelligent, ranking among the top five cognitively complex animals. They are raised extensively for pork and other products. Despite their reputation, pigs are naturally clean animals and prefer to cool themselves with water rather than mud.
animals.funFact: Pigs are considered to have the intelligence of a three-year-old human child and can learn to play video games using a joystick.

animals.name: Domestic Horse
animals.dangerNotes: Can kick or bite powerfully. Startled horses may rear or bolt. Requires experienced handling.
animals.description: The domestic horse has been one of humanity's most important working partners for over 5,000 years. Descended from wild Eurasian horses, they were first domesticated on the Pontic steppes and rapidly transformed human civilisation through transport, agriculture, and warfare. Today horses are kept for riding, sport, and companionship.
animals.funFact: Horses can sleep both standing up and lying down, and they need only around three hours of deep sleep per night.
aiNotesOrWarnings: primaryFoods is a general grazing/hay baseline; working and performance horses often receive supplementary grain feed.

animals.name: Domestic Goat
animals.dangerNotes: May headbutt. Horned individuals can cause minor injuries. Generally manageable.
animals.description: Domestic goats were among the first animals to be domesticated, roughly 10,000 years ago in the Zagros Mountains of Iran. Exceptionally adaptable, they thrive in environments from deserts to mountains. Goats are raised for milk, meat, fibre (cashmere and mohair), and skins. Their curious and independent nature makes them skilled escape artists.
animals.funFact: Goats have rectangular pupils that give them a 320-340 degree field of vision, helping them spot predators without moving their heads.

animals.name: Domestic Sheep
animals.dangerNotes: Rams can headbutt forcefully during mating season. Generally docile.
animals.description: Domestic sheep are among the earliest animals to be domesticated, with evidence dating back 10,000 years in Mesopotamia. There are over one billion sheep on Earth, making them one of the most numerous large mammals. Raised for wool, meat, and milk, sheep are highly social herd animals with a strong flocking instinct as a predator defence.
animals.funFact: Sheep can recognise and remember up to 50 individual sheep faces for over two years, and also remember human faces.

animals.name: House Mouse
animals.dangerNotes: Can carry diseases such as hantavirus and salmonella. Bites are rare but possible.
animals.description: The house mouse is one of the most widely distributed mammals on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica. Originally from Central Asia, it has spread globally by living in close association with humans. A highly adaptable commensal rodent, it thrives in buildings, farms, and urban environments. It is also the world's most commonly used laboratory animal.
animals.funFact: A female mouse can produce up to 10 litters of 5-6 pups per year, meaning a single pair can theoretically produce thousands of descendants annually.
aiNotesOrWarnings: Disease-vector content (hantavirus/salmonella) — keep any generated copy factual, avoid alarmist phrasing.
primaryFoods reflects commensal/opportunistic feeding near human structures, not a natural wild diet.

animals.name: Brown Rat
animals.dangerNotes: Can carry leptospirosis, hantavirus, and other pathogens. May bite if cornered.
animals.description: The brown rat is the largest and most widespread of the commensal rats, originally from northern China and now found on every continent except Antarctica. An exceptional burrower and swimmer, it colonises sewers, rubbish dumps, warehouses, and farmland. Brown rats are highly intelligent, demonstrating problem-solving ability and even showing empathy-like behaviour in laboratory studies.
animals.funFact: Brown rats communicate using ultrasonic vocalisations beyond human hearing range, and studies suggest they emit high-frequency 'laughter' when tickled or playing.
aiNotesOrWarnings: Disease-vector content (leptospirosis/hantavirus) — keep any generated copy factual, avoid alarmist phrasing.
primaryFoods reflects commensal/opportunistic feeding; diet is heavily dependent on proximity to human food waste.

animals.name: Black Rat
animals.dangerNotes: Historically a vector for bubonic plague via its fleas. Can carry salmonella and other pathogens.
animals.description: The black rat, also known as the ship rat or roof rat, is one of the world's most notorious invasive species. Originating in South and Southeast Asia, it spread globally via sailing ships and is considered a significant driver of island bird and reptile extinctions. Slender and agile, it prefers elevated locations - roof spaces, trees, and dense vegetation - in contrast to the burrowing brown rat.
animals.funFact: The black rat is believed to be the primary host responsible for spreading the bubonic plague pandemic ('Black Death') that killed a third of Europe's population in the 14th century.
aiNotesOrWarnings: References the Black Death / bubonic plague — historically sensitive content, keep factual and cited-style, no dramatization.
primaryFoods skews more arboreal/frugivorous than the Brown Rat, consistent with its tree- and roof-dwelling habits.

animals.name: Common Pigeon
animals.dangerNotes: No direct threat to humans. Droppings can be slippery and carry fungal spores (e.g. Cryptococcus) if accumulated in large quantities.
animals.description: The rock pigeon is the wild ancestor of all domestic and feral pigeons, originally native to sea cliffs and rocky outcrops across Europe, North Africa, and South Asia. Today it thrives in cities worldwide, where buildings mimic its ancestral cliff habitat. Pigeons have an extraordinary homing ability and were historically used to carry messages in wartime.
animals.funFact: Rock pigeons can navigate home from over 1,800 km away, detecting Earth's magnetic field and using the sun as a compass.
aiNotesOrWarnings: Source lifeSpanCaptiveYears (3-6) is really a general/free-living average for this species, not zoo-captive data — flag for SME review if that distinction matters downstream.

animals.name: House Sparrow
animals.description: The house sparrow is one of the most familiar and widespread birds in the world, having spread across every inhabited continent alongside human settlement. A small, sociable seed-eater, it nests in building crevices and dense shrubs close to human habitation. Despite its ubiquity, house sparrow populations have declined sharply in many European cities over recent decades.
animals.funFact: The house sparrow takes dust baths - vigorously flicking dry soil through its feathers - to help control parasites and maintain plumage condition.

animals.name: Domestic Chicken
animals.dangerNotes: Roosters may peck or spur if provoked. Chickens can carry Salmonella.
animals.description: The domestic chicken is the most numerous bird on Earth, with over 30 billion individuals worldwide. Descended from the red junglefowl of South and Southeast Asia, chickens were domesticated at least 8,000 years ago. They are raised globally for eggs and meat and display surprisingly complex social behaviour, including a pecking order hierarchy, tool use, and basic problem-solving.
animals.funFact: Chickens can remember and recognise over 100 individual faces of both chickens and humans.

animals.name: Domestic Duck
animals.dangerNotes: May nip if approached while nesting. Can carry Salmonella. Generally harmless.
animals.description: The domestic duck is descended from the mallard and has been kept by humans for at least 2,500 years, primarily for eggs, meat, and down feathers. Domestic ducks retain many of the behaviours of their wild ancestors, including dabbling for food in shallow water, preening, and strong waterproofing thanks to oil produced by the uropygial gland. They are sociable and do best kept in groups.
animals.funFact: A duck's quack does not echo - or rather, it does, but the quack naturally fades in and out in a way that makes the echo imperceptible to human ears.

animals.name: Donkey
animals.dangerNotes: May kick or bite if startled or mistreated. Generally docile and cautious rather than aggressive.
animals.description: The donkey is a domesticated member of the horse family descended from the African wild ass, first tamed in Africa or the Middle East around 5,000-7,000 years ago. Renowned for endurance and surefootedness on rough terrain, donkeys have long served as pack and draught animals in agriculture and trade. They are highly intelligent and cautious, often pausing to assess a situation rather than fleeing, a trait sometimes mistaken for stubbornness.
animals.funFact: A donkey's oversized ears help radiate heat to keep it cool and give it exceptional hearing, able to detect other donkeys from up to 3 kilometres away.
aiNotesOrWarnings: LifeSpanWildYears reflects feral/free-ranging populations, not truly wild ancestral populations. True wild Equus africanus is Critically Endangered and restricted to the Horn of Africa — tracked separately in the Africa regional dex, not here.

animals.name: Budgerigar
animals.dangerNotes: No threat to humans. May nip lightly if frightened while handled.
animals.description: The budgerigar is a small, nomadic parrot native to the dry interior of Australia, where wild flocks follow rainfall in search of seeding grasses. Widely kept as a pet since the 19th century, it is now one of the most popular cage birds in the world, bred into a huge range of colour mutations. Budgerigars are highly social and vocal, capable of mimicking sounds and human speech.
animals.funFact: In the wild, budgerigar flocks can number in the thousands and travel long distances, moving nomadically across the Australian outback in response to rain and food availability.
aiNotesOrWarnings: primaryFoods split between wild nomadic grass-seed foraging and typical captive/pet seed mixes.

animals.name: Guinea Pig
animals.dangerNotes: No threat to humans. May nip lightly if startled or mishandled.
primaryFoods: Pellet feed fortified with vitamin C
animals.description: The guinea pig is a domesticated rodent descended from wild cavies of the South American Andes, first tamed by indigenous peoples over 3,000 years ago for food and, later, companionship. Despite the name, it is neither a pig nor from Guinea. Today it is one of the most popular small pets worldwide, known for its sociable nature, wide variety of coat types, and distinctive range of vocalisations.
animals.funFact: Guinea pigs cannot synthesise their own vitamin C, much like humans, and require it from their diet to avoid scurvy.
aiNotesOrWarnings: LifeSpanWildYears reflects related wild cavy species, since true wild guinea pig populations are effectively extinct/undocumented.
Vitamin C fortification note added to primaryFoods since guinea pigs cannot synthesise it themselves (see existing lifespan note).

animals.name: Canary
animals.description: The canary is a small finch native to the Canary Islands, Azores, and Madeira, first taken into captivity by Spanish sailors in the 15th century and prized for its melodic, sustained song. Selective breeding over centuries produced numerous colour and song varieties now kept as pets worldwide, while wild populations persist in wooded and scrubby habitats across its native islands. Domesticated canaries were historically used in coal mines to detect toxic gases, owing to their sensitivity to airborne toxins.
animals.funFact: Canaries were used as living gas detectors in coal mines well into the 20th century, as their fast metabolism and small lungs made them collapse from carbon monoxide or methane long before it became dangerous to humans.
